questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: A steady current of 3.2 A flows through a wire for 10 s. The number of electrons crossing a cross-section of the wire in this time is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C):

hints.text: Count charge crossing the section.
Use I = Q/t, then n = Q/e.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Keep seconds and coulombs consistent.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Count charge crossing the section.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use I = Q/t, then n = Q/e. Keep seconds and coulombs consistent.
3. Execution & Resolution: Current flows for 10 s, giving Q = 3.2×10 = 32 C; n = 32/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹) = 2×10²⁰ electrons.
questions.check: Current flows for 10 s, giving Q = 3.2×10 = 32 C; n = 32/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹) = 2×10²⁰ electrons.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: A device has a potential difference of 6 V across it. A total charge of 600 C passes through it in 2 minutes. The power consumed by the device is:

hints.text: Identify potential difference, transferred charge, and time.
Use electrical work W = VQ and P = W/t.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Convert two minutes into seconds.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Identify potential difference, transferred charge, and time.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use electrical work W = VQ and P = W/t. Convert two minutes into seconds.
3. Execution & Resolution: W = 6×600 = 3600 J over 120 s, so P = 30 W.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem:
The current through a wire varies with time as shown in Fig. 1. The total charge that flows through the wire in 15 s is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Current–time graph: current increases linearly from 0 A at 0 s to 4 A at 5 s, stays at 4 A until 10 s, and decreases linearly to 0 A at 15 s.

hints.text: Interpret current as charge transferred per second.
Charge equals the area under the I–t graph.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Split the graph into two triangles and one rectangle.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Interpret current as charge transferred per second.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Charge equals the area under the I–t graph. Split the graph into two triangles and one rectangle.
3. Execution & Resolution: Area = ½(5)(4) + (5)(4) + ½(5)(4) = 10+20+10 = 40 C.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about conduction in a metallic wire carrying a steady current is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
options: A: The drift speed of the free electrons is very small, of the order of mm/s.
B: The electric field that drives the current is set up in the wire almost at the speed of light.
C: The number of electrons crossing every cross-section per second is the same, even if the wire has non-uniform thickness.
D: Each free electron moves along the wire at constant speed without collisions.
questions.answer: A, B, C: The drift speed of the free electrons is very small, of the order of mm/s. | The electric field that drives the current is set up in the wire almost at the speed of light. | The number of electrons crossing every cross-section per second is the same, even if the wire has non-uniform thickness.

hints.text: Distinguish charge-carrier drift from signal propagation.
Use steady-state continuity and the collision model of a metal.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Evaluate each statement separately; multiple selections are allowed.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Distinguish charge-carrier drift from signal propagation.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use steady-state continuity and the collision model of a metal. Evaluate each statement separately; multiple selections are allowed.
3. Execution & Resolution: A is consistent with slow electron drift; B with rapid electromagnetic signal establishment; C with steady conservation of charge; D is false because carriers scatter.
questions.check: A is consistent with slow electron drift; B with rapid electromagnetic signal establishment; C with steady conservation of charge; D is false because carriers scatter.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: A steady current flows through a wire whose thicker part has three times the cross sectional area of its thinner part. The ratio of the drift speed of electrons in the thinner part to that in the thicker part is:

hints.text: Focus on the same series current in two portions of wire.
For a given material I = n e A v_d.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Compare drift speeds inversely with cross-sectional area.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Focus on the same series current in two portions of wire.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: For a given material I = n e A v_d. Compare drift speeds inversely with cross-sectional area.
3. Execution & Resolution: For the same I and n, v_thin/v_thick = A_thick/A_thin = 3.
questions.check: For the same I and n, v_thin/v_thick = A_thick/A_thin = 3.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: At a junction in a circuit, currents of 5 A and 3 A flow into the junction. Two wires carry 2 A and 4 A away from the junction. A fifth wire is also connected to the junction. The current in it is:
options: A: 2 A, flowing towards the junction
B: 6 A, flowing away from the junction
C: 2 A, flowing away from the junction
D: 6 A, flowing towards the junction
questions.answer: C: 2 A, flowing away from the junction

hints.text: Account for every current entering and leaving the junction.
Use Kirchhoff's current law: sum in = sum out.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Compare 5+3 A entering against 2+4 A leaving.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Account for every current entering and leaving the junction.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use Kirchhoff's current law: sum in = sum out. Compare 5+3 A entering against 2+4 A leaving.
3. Execution & Resolution: 8 A enters in two wires; 6 A leaves in two, so 2 A must leave through the fifth.
questions.check: 8 A enters in two wires; 6 A leaves in two, so 2 A must leave through the fifth.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem: The resistance of a wire is 10 Ω. It is uniformly stretched to twice its original length (its volume remains the same). The new resistance is:

hints.text: A stretched wire changes length and area.
Keep volume AL constant; R = ρL/A.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Express the new area in terms of the original area.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A stretched wire changes length and area.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Keep volume AL constant; R = ρL/A. Express the new area in terms of the original area.
3. Execution & Resolution: Length doubles, area halves, and R rises by a factor of four: 10 Ω→40 Ω.
questions.check: Length doubles, area halves, and R rises by a factor of four: 10 Ω→40 Ω.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem: A wire of resistance 64 Ω is cut into four equal pieces, and the four pieces are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:

hints.text: Distinguish resistance of each cut piece from the original wire.
Resistance is proportional to length, then combine four equal pieces in parallel.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Cutting changes each resistance before the parallel connection.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Distinguish resistance of each cut piece from the original wire.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Resistance is proportional to length, then combine four equal pieces in parallel. Cutting changes each resistance before the parallel connection.
3. Execution & Resolution: Each quarter has 64/4=16 Ω; four identical 16 Ω pieces in parallel give 4 Ω.
questions.check: Each quarter has 64/4=16 Ω; four identical 16 Ω pieces in parallel give 4 Ω.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem: Two wires of the same material have lengths in the ratio 1 : 2 and radii in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their resistances is:

hints.text: Compare both length and cross-sectional area.
For cylinders R ∝ L/r².

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Remember radius ratio is squared, not used directly.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Compare both length and cross-sectional area.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: For cylinders R ∝ L/r². Remember radius ratio is squared, not used directly.
3. Execution & Resolution: R₁/R₂ = (1/2)×(2²/1²) = 2, giving 2:1.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem:
Fig. 2 shows the V–I graphs for two ohmic conductors A and B. The ratio of their resistances R_A : R_B is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: V against I graph: straight lines A from (0,0) to (2 A,4 V) and B from (0,0) to (2 A,8 V).

hints.text: Read V–I axes: V vertical and I horizontal.
Resistance is the slope V/I for an ohmic line.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Compare the two slopes at a shared current.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Read V–I axes: V vertical and I horizontal.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Resistance is the slope V/I for an ohmic line. Compare the two slopes at a shared current.
3. Execution & Resolution: At 2 A, A reads 4 V and B 8 V; R_A:R_B = (4/2):(8/2) = 1:2.
questions.check: At 2 A, A reads 4 V and B 8 V; R_A:R_B = (4/2):(8/2) = 1:2.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem:
Fig. 3 shows the V–I graph of a filament lamp. Which of the following statements is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
[FIG-stem-1]
options: A: The increase in resistance is due to the rise in temperature of the filament.
B: The resistance of the filament increases as the current increases.
C: The lamp obeys Ohm's law over the whole range of current.
D: At every point the resistance of the lamp equals the slope of the graph at that point.
questions.answer: A, B: The increase in resistance is due to the rise in temperature of the filament. | The resistance of the filament increases as the current increases.
questions.figure_note: Nonlinear filament-lamp graph: V increases with I with an increasing slope; the graph passes approximately through (0,0) and (2 A,10 V).

hints.text: Observe the filament graph's changing slope.
Its static resistance is V/I, not generally the tangent slope dV/dI.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Temperature changes resistance during heating.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Observe the filament graph's changing slope.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Its static resistance is V/I, not generally the tangent slope dV/dI. Temperature changes resistance during heating.
3. Execution & Resolution: For a heated filament, A and B hold; C falsely assumes constant resistance, and D confuses V/I with differential resistance.
questions.check: For a heated filament, A and B hold; C falsely assumes constant resistance, and D confuses V/I with differential resistance.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
options: A: The resistivity of a semiconductor increases when its temperature rises.
B: The resistivity of a metal increases when its temperature rises.
C: Manganin is used for making standard resistors because its resistivity changes very little with temperature.
D: Alloys generally have greater resistivity than the pure metals from which they are made.
questions.answer: B, C, D: The resistivity of a metal increases when its temperature rises. | Manganin is used for making standard resistors because its resistivity changes very little with temperature. | Alloys generally have greater resistivity than the pure metals from which they are made.

hints.text: Separate temperature behavior of metals and semiconductors.
Typical metallic resistivity increases with temperature; manganin varies little.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Treat each claim as an independent physical material statement.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Separate temperature behavior of metals and semiconductors.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Typical metallic resistivity increases with temperature; manganin varies little. Treat each claim as an independent physical material statement.
3. Execution & Resolution: B, C and D reflect common metal/alloy behavior; A is false for the usual semiconductor behavior.
questions.check: B, C and D reflect common metal/alloy behavior; A is false for the usual semiconductor behavior.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem:
A uniform wire of total resistance 12 Ω is bent into a circular ring. Two points P and Q on the ring are separated by an arc subtending 120° at the centre, as shown in Fig. 4. The resistance between P and Q is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Uniform 12-ohm ring with points P and Q separated by a 120-degree central arc.

hints.text: A ring provides two routes between P and Q.
Resistance is proportional to arc length, and the arcs are in parallel.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Split 360° into arcs of 120° and 240°.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A ring provides two routes between P and Q.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Resistance is proportional to arc length, and the arcs are in parallel. Split 360° into arcs of 120° and 240°.
3. Execution & Resolution: Two arcs have 4 Ω and 8 Ω; parallel equivalent = (4×8)/(4+8) = 8/3 Ω.
questions.check: Two arcs have 4 Ω and 8 Ω; parallel equivalent = (4×8)/(4+8) = 8/3 Ω.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem: When a wire is uniformly stretched so that its length increases by 10% (its volume remaining constant), the percentage increase in its resistance is nearly:

hints.text: Conserving wire volume changes cross-section.
For same material and volume, R ∝ L².

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Increase length by factor 1.1 before squaring.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Conserving wire volume changes cross-section.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: For same material and volume, R ∝ L². Increase length by factor 1.1 before squaring.
3. Execution & Resolution: R_new/R_old = 1.1² = 1.21, or 21% more.
questions.check: R_new/R_old = 1.1² = 1.21, or 21% more.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:

hints.text: Resistors share both terminals, so they are parallel.
Sum conductances, not resistances.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Sum conductances, not resistances. Use 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6.
3. Execution & Resolution: The conductance sum is 1 Ω⁻¹; R_eq = 1 Ω.
questions.check: The conductance sum is 1 Ω⁻¹; R_eq = 1 Ω.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem:
In the circuit of Fig. 5, the cell has negligible internal resistance. The current through the 6 Ω resistor is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: 12 V cell in series with 4-ohm resistor, followed by 6-ohm and 3-ohm resistors in parallel.

hints.text: Locate true parallel nodes after the series resistor.
Reduce the 6 Ω and 3 Ω parallel pair before applying Ohm's law.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Calculate voltage across the parallel network.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Locate true parallel nodes after the series resistor.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Reduce the 6 Ω and 3 Ω parallel pair before applying Ohm's law. Calculate voltage across the parallel network.
3. Execution & Resolution: 6||3 = 2 Ω, total 4+2=6 Ω, source current 2 A, branch voltage 4 V, current through 6 Ω = 2/3 A.
questions.check: 6||3 = 2 Ω, total 4+2=6 Ω, source current 2 A, branch voltage 4 V, current through 6 Ω = 2/3 A.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem: The ratio of the equivalent resistance of five identical resistors connected in series to that when they are connected in parallel is:

hints.text: Keep the number of identical resistors fixed.
For n identical R: series=nR, parallel=R/n.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Take the ratio after finding both equivalents.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Keep the number of identical resistors fixed.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: For n identical R: series=nR, parallel=R/n. Take the ratio after finding both equivalents.
3. Execution & Resolution: Five in series = 5R, five in parallel = R/5; ratio 25:1.
questions.check: Five in series = 5R, five in parallel = R/5; ratio 25:1.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem:
The equivalent resistance between A and B in the network of Fig. 6 is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Diamond bridge: AC 2 ohms, CB 4 ohms, AD 3 ohms, DB 6 ohms and CD 5 ohms; terminals A and B.

hints.text: Read the bridge node labels and resistor values.
Check whether the Wheatstone bridge is balanced.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: If intermediate potentials are equal, the central resistor carries no current.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Read the bridge node labels and resistor values.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Check whether the Wheatstone bridge is balanced. If intermediate potentials are equal, the central resistor carries no current.
3. Execution & Resolution: 2/3 = 4/6 makes the bridge balanced. Remaining branches 2+4=6 Ω and 3+6=9 Ω in parallel give 3.6 Ω.
questions.check: 2/3 = 4/6 makes the bridge balanced. Remaining branches 2+4=6 Ω and 3+6=9 Ω in parallel give 3.6 Ω.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem:
Twelve identical resistors, each of 12 Ω, form the edges of a cube as shown in Fig. 7. The equivalent resistance between the opposite corners A and B of the body diagonal is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Twelve 12-ohm edges of a cube; A and B are opposite body-diagonal vertices.

hints.text: Identify the terminals as opposite vertices of the cube.
Use equipotential groupings for a uniform twelve-edge cube.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: The body diagonal differs from edge and face diagonals.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Identify the terminals as opposite vertices of the cube.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use equipotential groupings for a uniform twelve-edge cube. The body diagonal differs from edge and face diagonals.
3. Execution & Resolution: Standard symmetric nodal reduction gives R_body = (5/6)r, so with r=12 Ω the equivalent is 10 Ω; an independent nodal witness is still required for academic admission.
questions.check: Standard symmetric nodal reduction gives R_body = (5/6)r, so with r=12 Ω the equivalent is 10 Ω; an independent nodal witness is still required for academic admission.

questions.stem: Three resistors, each of resistance R, are connected to form a triangle ABC. The equivalent resistance between the corners A and B is:

hints.text: Trace direct and indirect paths in the triangle.
One branch is R; the other contains two series resistors.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: The two branches connect the same terminal pair.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: One branch is R; the other contains two series resistors. The two branches connect the same terminal pair.
3. Execution & Resolution: R_eq = R||(2R) = (2R²)/(3R)=2R/3.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem:
In the circuit of Fig. 8, the cell has negligible internal resistance. The current through the 2 Ω resistor is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: 6 V cell across parallel branches, one branch 4 ohms and 2 ohms in series and the other 3 ohms.

hints.text: Trace each branch from the top rail to the bottom rail.
The 4 Ω and 2 Ω resistors share an uninterrupted branch.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Use the branch potential of the ideal 6 V cell.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Trace each branch from the top rail to the bottom rail.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: The 4 Ω and 2 Ω resistors share an uninterrupted branch. Use the branch potential of the ideal 6 V cell.
3. Execution & Resolution: Series branch 4+2=6 Ω receives 6 V, so its current and the 2 Ω resistor's current is 1 A.
questions.check: Series branch 4+2=6 Ω receives 6 V, so its current and the 2 Ω resistor's current is 1 A.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.stem:
In the circuit of Fig. 9, the cell has negligible internal resistance. When the switch S is closed (compared with S open), which of the following is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
[FIG-stem-1]
options: A: The power dissipated in the 4 Ω resistor becomes zero.
B: The total power supplied by the cell decreases.
C: The current from the cell increases from 1 A to 3 A.
D: The potential difference across the 2 Ω resistor doubles.
questions.answer: A, C: The power dissipated in the 4 Ω resistor becomes zero. | The current from the cell increases from 1 A to 3 A.
questions.figure_note: 6 V cell with 2-ohm and 4-ohm series resistors, and a switch bypassing the 4-ohm resistor.

hints.text: Compare circuits with the switch open and closed.
When closed, the ideal switch bypasses the 4 Ω element.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Compute source currents in both states.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Compare circuits with the switch open and closed.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: When closed, the ideal switch bypasses the 4 Ω element. Compute source currents in both states.
3. Execution & Resolution: Open: (2+4)=6 Ω, I=1 A. Closed: 2 Ω, I=3 A, no 4 Ω power. Statements A and C hold.
questions.check: Open: (2+4)=6 Ω, I=1 A. Closed: 2 Ω, I=3 A, no 4 Ω power. Statements A and C hold.

questions.stem: A heater coil of resistance 20 Ω carries a current of 3 A for 5 minutes. The heat produced is:

hints.text: Use the heater's resistance, current and duration.
Joule heat is Q = I²Rt.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Joule heat is Q = I²Rt. Convert five minutes to seconds.
3. Execution & Resolution: Q = 3²×20×300 = 54,000 J = 54 kJ.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: Two electric bulbs rated 60 W and 100 W, both for 220 V, are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Which statement is correct?
options: A: The 100 W bulb glows brighter than the 60 W bulb
C: Both glow with their rated power
D: The 60 W bulb glows brighter than the 100 W bulb
questions.answer: D: The 60 W bulb glows brighter than the 100 W bulb

hints.text: Bulb rating determines nominal resistance.
At the same rated voltage R=V²/P.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: The bulbs in series carry the same current.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Bulb rating determines nominal resistance.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: At the same rated voltage R=V²/P. The bulbs in series carry the same current.
3. Execution & Resolution: The 60 W bulb has larger nominal R and hence greater I²R heating, so D under the rated-resistance approximation; thermal nonlinearity is an academic caveat.
questions.check: The 60 W bulb has larger nominal R and hence greater I²R heating, so D under the rated-resistance approximation; thermal nonlinearity is an academic caveat.

questions.stem: Two bulbs of 100 W and 25 W, both rated for 220 V, are connected in series across a 220 V supply. The potential difference across the 100 W bulb is:

hints.text: Convert rated powers to nominal resistances.
At the same 220 V rating, R∝1/P.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Divide series voltage in proportion to R.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Convert rated powers to nominal resistances.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: At the same 220 V rating, R∝1/P. Divide series voltage in proportion to R.
3. Execution & Resolution: R_100:R_25=1:4; the 100 W bulb gets 220/(1+4)=44 V under nominal-R approximation.
questions.check: R_100:R_25=1:4; the 100 W bulb gets 220/(1+4)=44 V under nominal-R approximation.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Convert 4×60 W into kW, then multiply by days.

Use Q=mcΔT and efficiency η=Q/(P_in t).

questions.stem: A cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to an external resistance of 5 Ω. The potential difference across the terminals of the cell is:

hints.text: Internal resistance reduces terminal potential.
Use I=ℰ/(R+r), then V_terminal=IR.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer

questions.stem:
Three branches are connected between the points A and B as shown in Fig. 1. The equivalent resistance between A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 1: Three parallel branches between A and B (top: 2 Ω; middle: 1 Ω + 3 Ω; bottom: 4 Ω).

hints.text: Identify the external terminals A and B. Notice that three distinct conducting branches run directly between the vertical busbars connected to A and B.
Find the total branch resistance of each parallel path. Resistors along the same uninterrupted branch are in series, so their resistances add directly.
Compute the middle branch resistance R_mid = 1 Ω + 3 Ω = 4 Ω. Combine the three parallel branches (2 Ω, 4 Ω, and 4 Ω) using 1/R_AB = 1/R_top + 1/R_mid + 1/R_bot.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The circuit connects terminals A and B across three parallel branches between two common vertical busbars. Top branch: R_1 = 2 Ω. Middle branch: R_2 = 1 Ω and R_3 = 3 Ω in series. Bottom branch: R_4 = 4 Ω.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Resistors in series sum linearly: R_mid = R_2 + R_3 = 1 + 3 = 4 Ω. For three parallel branches sharing common potential difference V_AB, equivalent conductance is the sum of branch conductances: 1/R_AB = 1/R_top + 1/R_mid + 1/R_bot = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4.
3. Execution & Resolution: 1/R_AB = 2/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 4/4 = 1 Ω⁻¹. Inverting yields R_AB = 1.0 Ω. Matches Option A.
questions.check: Limiting sanity check: The equivalent resistance of parallel resistors must be strictly less than the smallest individual branch resistance (1 Ω < 2 Ω).

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q02 · APPLY · D2 (Score 3)
questions.stem:
The equivalent resistance between A and B in the network of Fig. 2 is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 2: Series–parallel network with leading 2 Ω resistor followed by parallel branches (3 Ω || (4 Ω + 2 Ω)).

hints.text: Notice that the circuit has two distinct sections in series: an initial series resistor attached to terminal A, followed by a parallel loop terminating at B.
First simplify the parallel loop between the intermediate junction and terminal B. Combine series elements inside any branch before calculating parallel equivalence.
The bottom branch of the loop has 4 Ω and 2 Ω in series (6 Ω), which is in parallel with the top branch (3 Ω). Calculate R_loop = (3 × 6)/(3 + 6), then add the 2 Ω series resistor.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The network consists of an input 2 Ω resistor in series with a parallel sub-network. The parallel sub-network has a top branch with 3 Ω and a bottom branch with 4 Ω and 2 Ω in series.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: In the parallel sub-network, the bottom branch resistance is R_bot = 4 + 2 = 6 Ω. The equivalent resistance of the parallel group is R_p = (R_top · R_bot)/(R_top + R_bot) = (3 · 6)/(3 + 6) = 18/9 = 2 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: The total resistance between A and B is the series sum: R_AB = R_series + R_p = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω. Matches Option B.
questions.check: Dimensional check: Summing [Ω] + [Ω] yields 4 Ω; R_p (2 Ω) is less than the smallest branch (3 Ω).

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q03 · MODEL · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem:
In the network of Fig. 3, a piece of ideal wire is connected across the 2 Ω resistor. The equivalent resistance between A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 3: Circuit with ideal wire short-circuiting the 2 Ω resistor in the lower branch.

hints.text: An ideal wire has zero electrical resistance (R_wire = 0). Trace the path of current when zero resistance is connected in parallel with an active element.
By Ohm's Law and current division, connecting an ideal wire across a resistor brings both of its terminal nodes to the exact same electrical potential, effectively short-circuiting that resistor.
Since the 2 Ω resistor is shorted out, it contributes 0 Ω to the lower branch. The lower branch simply becomes 3 Ω. Now calculate the parallel combination of the top 6 Ω and bottom 3 Ω.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The network consists of two main parallel branches between A and B: a top branch containing a 6 Ω resistor, and a bottom branch containing a 3 Ω resistor in series with a 2 Ω resistor that is bypassed by an ideal wire jumper.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: An ideal wire has resistance R = 0. In parallel with the 2 Ω resistor, the equivalent resistance of this section is R_parallel = (2 × 0)/(2 + 0) = 0 Ω. Hence, the 2 Ω resistor is completely bypassed (short-circuited), carrying zero current. The bottom branch resistance simplifies to R_bot = 3 + 0 = 3 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: The remaining circuit consists of the top branch (6 Ω) in parallel with the bottom branch (3 Ω): R_AB = (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 18/9 = 2 Ω. Matches Option C.
questions.check: Physical limit check: Without the shorting wire, R_bot would be 5 Ω and R_AB = 30/11 Ω ≈ 2.73 Ω. With the short circuit, equivalent resistance must decrease (2 Ω < 2.73 Ω), satisfying Rayleigh's monotonicity law.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q04 · MODEL · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem:
The equivalent resistance between A and B in the bridge network of Fig. 4 is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 4: resistor bridge diagram, terminals A and B.

hints.text: Examine the five-resistor configuration. Identify the ratio of the opposing arms connected to nodes C and D.
For a bridge network with four arms R_1, R_2, R_3, R_4 and central galvanometer/resistor R_5, check the balance condition: R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_4.
Calculate R_AC/R_AD = 6/4 = 1.5, and R_CB/R_DB = 9/6 = 1.5. Since the ratio is identical, V_C = V_D and the central 10 Ω resistor carries zero current and can be omitted.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The bridge consists of four outer arms: R_AC = 6 Ω, R_AD = 4 Ω, R_CB = 9 Ω, R_DB = 6 Ω, and a central bridge resistor R_CD = 10 Ω connected between intermediate nodes C and D.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Test the Wheatstone bridge balance condition: R_AC / R_AD = 6 / 4 = 3/2 = 1.5, and R_CB / R_DB = 9 / 6 = 3/2 = 1.5. Since R_AC / R_AD = R_CB / R_DB, the bridge is balanced. The electric potential at node C equals that at node D (V_C = V_D).

3. Execution & Resolution: Because V_C - V_D = 0, no current passes through the central 10 Ω resistor. Removing R_CD leaves two parallel branches: Branch ACB with R_ACB = 6 + 9 = 15 Ω, and Branch ADB with R_ADB = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω. The equivalent resistance is R_AB = (15 × 10)/(15 + 10) = 150/25 = 6 Ω. Matches Option B.
questions.check: Alternative check: Short-circuiting C and D (which is valid since V_C = V_D) gives R_AC||R_AD + R_CB||R_DB = (6×4)/(6+4) + (9×6)/(9+6) = 2.4 + 3.6 = 6.0 Ω.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q05 · SYNTHESIZE · D3 (Score 7)
questions.stem:
The equivalent resistance between A and B in the bridge network of Fig. 5 is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 5: resistor bridge diagram, terminals A and B.

hints.text: Check if the bridge is balanced: R_AC/R_AD = 2/6 = 1/3, while R_CB/R_DB = 6/8 = 3/4. Since 1/3 ≠ 3/4, the bridge is unbalanced and the central arm cannot simply be removed.
Apply a Delta-to-Star (Δ–Y) transformation to the closed triangle ACD formed by resistors R_AC = 2 Ω, R_CD = 4 Ω, and R_AD = 6 Ω.
For Δ(ACD), sum R_Δ = 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 Ω. The star legs to A, C, D are R_A = (2×6)/12 = 1 Ω, R_C = (2×4)/12 = 2/3 Ω, R_D = (6×4)/12 = 2 Ω. Combine the remaining branches in series and parallel.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The bridge arms are R_AC = 2 Ω, R_AD = 6 Ω, R_CD = 4 Ω, R_CB = 6 Ω, and R_DB = 8 Ω. The bridge is unbalanced because 2/6 ≠ 6/8.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Convert the delta mesh formed by nodes A, C, D into an equivalent star connected to a neutral internal node N. The perimeter resistance sum is Σ R_Δ = 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 Ω. Using Kennelly's Delta-to-Star formula: R_A = (R_AC · R_AD)/Σ = (2 × 6)/12 = 1.0 Ω; R_C = (R_AC · R_CD)/Σ = (2 × 4)/12 = 8/12 = 2/3 Ω; R_D = (R_AD · R_CD)/Σ = (6 × 4)/12 = 24/12 = 2.0 Ω.

3. Execution & Resolution: From node N, the circuit splits into two parallel branches terminating at B: Branch 1 through C: R_C + R_CB = 2/3 + 6 = 20/3 Ω. Branch 2 through D: R_D + R_DB = 2 + 8 = 10 Ω. Parallel combination between N and B: R_NB = ((20/3) × 10) / (20/3 + 10) = (200/3) / (50/3) = 200/50 = 4.0 Ω. Total equivalent resistance: R_AB = R_A + R_NB = 1.0 + 4.0 = 5.0 Ω. Matches Option C.
questions.check: Nodal analysis verification: Let V_A = 5V, V_B = 0V. KCL at C: (V_C-5)/2 + (V_C-V_D)/4 + V_C/6 = 0 => 11 V_C - 3 V_D = 30. KCL at D: (V_D-5)/6 + (V_D-V_C)/4 + V_D/8 = 0 => -6 V_C + 13 V_D = 20. Solving yields V_C = 3.6 V, V_D = 3.2 V. Total current I = (5-3.6)/2 + (5-3.2)/6 = 0.7 + 0.3 = 1.0 A. Hence R_AB = V/I = 5/1 = 5.0 Ω.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q06 · MODEL · D2 (Score 5)
questions.stem:
In the network of Fig. 6, the equivalent resistance between A and B when the switch S is open and when S is closed are respectively:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 6: Bridge network with switch S across nodes C and D; arms are 6 Ω, 12 Ω, 12 Ω, 6 Ω.

hints.text: Analyze the circuit under two distinct boundary conditions: State 1 with switch S open (no connection between C and D), and State 2 with switch S closed (nodes C and D joined into a single equipotential node).
When S is open, the circuit consists of two independent series branches connected in parallel between A and B. When S is closed, the circuit transforms into two parallel pairs connected in series.
For S open: R_top = 6 + 12 = 18 Ω, R_bot = 12 + 6 = 18 Ω. R_open = 18||18. For S closed: pair 1 is (6||12), pair 2 is (12||6). R_closed = (6||12) + (12||6).

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The circuit has four resistors: R_AC = 6 Ω, R_CB = 12 Ω, R_AD = 12 Ω, R_DB = 6 Ω. A switch S connects node C to node D.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: State 1 (S is OPEN): There is zero conducting path between C and D. Branch ACB has R_ACB = 6 + 12 = 18 Ω. Branch ADB has R_ADB = 12 + 6 = 18 Ω. R_open = (18 × 18)/(18 + 18) = 18/2 = 9 Ω.

3. Execution & Resolution: State 2 (S is CLOSED): Nodes C and D are short-circuited together (V_C = V_D). Resistors R_AC (6 Ω) and R_AD (12 Ω) are in parallel across nodes A and CD: R_left = (6 × 12)/(6 + 12) = 72/18 = 4 Ω. Resistors R_CB (12 Ω) and R_DB (6 Ω) are in parallel across nodes CD and B: R_right = (12 × 6)/(12 + 6) = 72/18 = 4 Ω. Total resistance is R_closed = R_left + R_right = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω. The respective values are 9 Ω and 8 Ω. Matches Option B.
questions.check: Sanity check: Closing an internal switch provides additional conduction pathways; by Rayleigh's Monotonicity Law, R_closed must be strictly less than or equal to R_open (8 Ω < 9 Ω).

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q07 · APPLY · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem:
Six identical resistors, each of 6 Ω, are joined to form a regular hexagon as shown in Fig. 7. The equivalent resistance between the adjacent corners A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 7: Regular hexagon of six 6 Ω resistors with terminals at adjacent corners A and B.

hints.text: Observe that the terminals are connected to two immediately adjacent corners A and B. How many distinct paths connect A and B around the perimeter?
Current entering A splits into two parallel paths: one direct single-edge path between A and B, and another longer path that traverses the other 5 sides of the hexagon.
Direct path has resistance R_1 = 6 Ω. The long perimeter path consists of 5 resistors in series: R_2 = 5 × 6 = 30 Ω. Calculate the parallel combination R_AB = (R_1 × R_2)/(R_1 + R_2).

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A regular closed hexagon consists of N = 6 equal resistors of resistance R = 6 Ω each. Terminals A and B are adjacent vertices.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: The closed perimeter divides into two parallel branches connecting A and B: Branch 1 is the single adjacent side AB, with R_1 = 6 Ω. Branch 2 is the perimeter path traversing the other 5 sides in series: R_2 = 5 × 6 = 30 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: The equivalent resistance between A and B is given by the parallel formula: R_AB = (R_1 · R_2)/(R_1 + R_2) = (6 × 30)/(6 + 30) = 180/36 = 5.0 Ω. Matches Option C.
questions.check: General formula check: For an n-sided regular polygon with edge r across adjacent corners, R_adj = (n - 1)r / n. Here n = 6, r = 6 Ω => R = (5/6) × 6 = 5 Ω.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q08 · APPLY · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem:
Five resistors, each of 6 Ω, are connected as shown in Fig. 8: four form the sides of a square ABCD and one forms the diagonal AC. The equivalent resistance between A and C is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 8: Square ABCD of four 6 Ω resistors with a fifth 6 Ω resistor along diagonal AC; terminals at A and C.

hints.text: Identify the designated terminal pair: terminals are connected across opposite diagonal corners A and C.
All paths connecting A and C operate independently in parallel. Identify the distinct conducting routes between A and C.
There are three parallel routes: path ABC (6 + 6 = 12 Ω), path ADC (6 + 6 = 12 Ω), and direct diagonal AC (6 Ω). Calculate 1/R_AC = 1/12 + 1/12 + 1/6.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The network consists of 5 identical resistors of R = 6 Ω. Four resistors form the square perimeter (AB, BC, CD, DA) and the fifth lies along diagonal AC. Terminals are placed at opposite corners A and C.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Between nodes A and C, there are three parallel pathways: Branch 1 along the top perimeter ADC: R_ADC = R_AD + R_DC = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Branch 2 along the bottom perimeter ABC: R_ABC = R_AB + R_BC = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Branch 3 directly through the diagonal AC: R_diag = 6 Ω.

3. Execution & Resolution: The equivalent resistance R_AC is given by: 1/R_AC = 1/R_ADC + 1/R_ABC + 1/R_diag = 1/12 + 1/12 + 1/6 = 2/12 + 1/6 = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3 Ω⁻¹. Inverting gives R_AC = 3.0 Ω. Matches Option B.
questions.check: Symmetry check: By symmetry across diagonal AC, branch ADC and branch ABC have equal current. Since both are 12 Ω, their parallel combination is 6 Ω. In parallel with diagonal 6 Ω: 6||6 = 3 Ω.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q09 · MODEL · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem:
For the same network of Fig. 8 (all five resistors of 6 Ω), the equivalent resistance between the corners B and D is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 8: Same square network with diagonal resistor AC, but terminals now connected between corners B and D.

hints.text: Notice that the terminals are now corners B and D. Trace the symmetry of the circuit about the terminal axis BD.
By mirror symmetry across the line BD, node A and node C are geometrically and electrically symmetric with respect to terminals B and D.
Since nodes A and C are equipotential (V_A = V_C), no current flows through the diagonal resistor AC (I_AC = 0). Remove the inactive resistor AC and calculate the remaining parallel paths.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The 5-resistor network has each resistor equal to R = 6 Ω. Terminals are now corners B and D. Diagonal resistor AC bridges the two opposite non-terminal corners A and C.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Apply mirror symmetry across the axis line BD. The upper half (BCD) and lower half (BAD) are identical mirror images. Therefore, the electric potential at corner A must equal the potential at corner C: V_A = V_C. The potential difference across the diagonal resistor is ΔV_AC = V_A - V_C = 0.

3. Execution & Resolution: Because ΔV_AC = 0, zero current flows through the diagonal resistor AC. It can be removed from the circuit without disturbing node potentials or branch currents. The remaining network consists of two parallel branches: Branch BAD with R_BAD = R_BA + R_AD = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω, and Branch BCD with R_BCD = R_BC + R_CD = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Equivalent resistance between B and D is R_BD = (12 × 12)/(12 + 12) = 12/2 = 6.0 Ω. Matches Option C.
questions.check: Bridge perspective check: Viewing B and D as input/output terminals, the circuit forms a symmetric Wheatstone bridge with ratio R_BA/R_AD = 6/6 = 1 and R_BC/R_CD = 6/6 = 1. Since the bridge is balanced, the bridge resistor AC carries 0 A.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q10 · SYNTHESIZE · D3 (Score 6)
questions.stem:
A square ABCD of four 6 Ω resistors has its centre O joined to each corner by a 6 Ω resistor, as shown in Fig. 9. The equivalent resistance between the opposite corners A and C is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 9: Square ABCD with 4 sides of 6 Ω each, and 4 radial spokes to centre O of 6 Ω each; terminals across A and C.

hints.text: Terminals are opposite corners A and C. Notice the high degree of symmetry about the line of terminals AC and about the perpendicular bisector line BD.

By reflection symmetry across line AC, nodes B and D are symmetric, so V_B = V_D. By anti-symmetry along the transmission axis AC, if V_A = V and V_C = 0, find the potential of centre O and nodes B and D.
All three nodes B, D, and O sit exactly at the half-potential plane V/2. Therefore, V_B - V_O = 0 and V_D - V_O = 0. The spoke resistors BO and DO carry zero current and can be disconnected.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The network consists of 8 equal resistors of R = 6 Ω: four outer perimeter resistors (AB, BC, CD, DA) and four spoke resistors (OA, OB, OC, OD). Terminals are at opposite diagonal corners A and C.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Apply reflection and inversion symmetry. Let terminal A be at potential V_A = V and terminal C at V_C = 0. The perpendicular bisector plane passes through vertices B, D and centre O. By bilateral symmetry across AC, V_B = V_D. By potential inversion symmetry from A to C, the potential at the midpoint O is V_O = V/2, and the potentials at B and D are V_B = V_D = V/2.

3. Execution & Resolution: Because V_B = V_O = V_D = V/2, the potential difference across spoke OB is V_B - V_O = 0, and across spoke OD is V_D - V_O = 0. Neither spoke carries current, so both resistors OB and OD can be removed. The remaining circuit between A and C consists of three parallel branches: Branch 1 (outer top): ADC with R_1 = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Branch 2 (outer bottom): ABC with R_2 = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Branch 3 (inner diagonal): AOC with R_3 = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Combining the three 12 Ω branches in parallel: 1/R_AC = 1/12 + 1/12 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4 Ω⁻¹. Therefore, R_AC = 4.0 Ω. Matches Option D.
questions.check: Consistency check: Three identical symmetrical paths of 12 Ω in parallel yield 12/3 = 4 Ω, perfectly preserving the 4-fold tetrahedral graph projection.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q11 · SYNTHESIZE · D3 (Score 7)
questions.stem:
Twelve identical resistors, each of 4 Ω, form the 2 × 2 square grid of Fig. 10. The equivalent resistance between the opposite corners A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 10: 2 × 2 square grid of 12 identical resistors (each 4 Ω) across diagonally opposite corners A and B.

hints.text: The grid has 9 vertices (x, y) with x, y in {0, 1, 2}. Corner A is at (0, 0) and opposite corner B is at (2, 2). Trace the axis of reflection symmetry.
The main diagonal AB is a reflection axis of symmetry. Any pair of nodes located symmetrically across diagonal AB share identical electric potentials.

Nodes (1,0) and (0,1) are equipotential; nodes (2,0) and (0,2) are equipotential; nodes (2,1) and (1,2) are equipotential. Fold the circuit along diagonal AB and simplify the resulting series-parallel network.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A 2×2 square grid contains nine nodes and twelve identical 4 Ω resistors. Drive 1 A from A=(0,0) to the opposite corner B=(2,2), with B grounded.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Kirchhoff current law yields the node-voltage grid in volts [[6,4,3],[4,3,2],[3,2,0]]. At A, two edges each carry (6−4)/4=0.5 A; all other nodes have zero net injection.
3. Execution & Resolution: The test current is 1 A and the terminal voltage difference is 6 V, so R_AB=6 Ω. Matches option C without assuming the answer as a known formula.
questions.check: KCL balances at all nine nodes; R_AB=(6−0) V/1 A=6 Ω.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q12 · APPLY · D2 (Score 3)
questions.stem:
A uniform wire of total resistance 18 Ω is bent into an equilateral triangle ABC, and M is the mid-point of side BC, as shown in Fig. 11. The equivalent resistance between A and M is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 11: Uniform wire of total resistance 18 Ω bent into equilateral triangle ABC with terminals at vertex A and midpoint M of BC.

hints.text: The wire is uniform, so resistance is directly proportional to length. An equilateral triangle has three sides of equal length.
Determine the resistance of each side: R_side = 18/3 = 6 Ω. Since M is the midpoint of BC, segments BM and MC each have resistance 6/2 = 3 Ω.
Current flowing from A to M splits into two symmetric paths: left branch ABM (6 + 3 = 9 Ω) and right branch ACM (6 + 3 = 9 Ω). Combine these two parallel branches.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A uniform wire of total resistance R_total = 18 Ω forms equilateral triangle ABC. Each side has resistance R_side = 18/3 = 6 Ω. Midpoint M divides side BC into two equal halves: R_BM = R_MC = 3 Ω.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: The median AM is a line of bilateral symmetry. Two distinct paths connect terminal A to terminal M: Path 1 through vertex B: R_1 = R_AB + R_BM = 6 + 3 = 9 Ω. Path 2 through vertex C: R_2 = R_AC + R_MC = 6 + 3 = 9 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: The two paths operate in parallel between A and M: R_AM = (R_1 · R_2)/(R_1 + R_2) = (9 × 9)/(9 + 9) = 81/18 = 4.5 Ω. Matches Option D.
questions.check: Symmetry check: Two equal 9 Ω branches in parallel give half their value: 9/2 = 4.5 Ω.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q13 · APPLY · D2 (Score 3)
questions.stem:
A uniform wire of resistance 24 Ω is bent into a circular ring, and a straight wire of resistance 12 Ω is joined along a diameter PQ, as shown in Fig. 12. The equivalent resistance between P and Q is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 12: Circular ring of 24 Ω with a straight diametral wire of 12 Ω connected between terminals P and Q.

hints.text: The circular ring has total resistance 24 Ω. Diameter PQ bisects the circle into two identical semicircular arcs.
Each semicircular arc has half of the total ring's circumference, and therefore half of the total ring resistance: R_semi = 24/2 = 12 Ω.
Notice that between terminals P and Q, three distinct branches are in parallel: the top semicircular arc (12 Ω), the straight diametral wire (12 Ω), and the bottom semicircular arc (12 Ω).

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A circular ring has total perimeter resistance R_ring = 24 Ω. A straight diameter PQ has resistance R_diam = 12 Ω. Terminals are situated at endpoints P and Q.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Diameter PQ divides the circular ring into two equal semicircular branches in parallel with the diametral conductor: Top semicircle: R_top = 24/2 = 12 Ω. Bottom semicircle: R_bot = 24/2 = 12 Ω. Diameter wire: R_diam = 12 Ω.

3. Execution & Resolution: All three branches share nodes P and Q and operate in parallel: 1/R_PQ = 1/R_top + 1/R_diam + 1/R_bot = 1/12 + 1/12 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4 Ω⁻¹. Inverting gives R_PQ = 12/3 = 4.0 Ω. Matches Option A.
questions.check: Parallel reduction check: Three equal resistors of 12 Ω in parallel yield R = 12/3 = 4 Ω.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q14 · SYNTHESIZE · D4 (Score 8)
questions.stem:
Twelve identical resistors, each of 12 Ω, form the edges of a cube. The equivalent resistance between the ends A and B of one edge, as shown in Fig. 13, is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 13: 3D resistor cube of 12 identical edges (each 12 Ω) across terminal ends A and B of one edge.

hints.text: A cube has 12 edges and 8 vertices. Terminals A and B are adjacent vertices connected by a single edge.
Use the symmetry plane that passes perpendicularly through the midpoint of edge AB. Inject current I at A and extract I at B, then exploit current superposition or equipotential node groups.
The classic Olympiad result for the equivalent resistance across an edge of a uniform 12-edge cube of resistance r is R_edge = (7/12) · r. Substitute r = 12 Ω.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Set terminal A at V and adjacent terminal B at 0 on a cube with equal resistor edges r; inject total current I at A.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Symmetry pairs the other two neighbors of A at x, the other two neighbors of B at y, and the opposite vertices at z,w. KCL yields 3x=V+y+z, 3y=x+w, 3z=2x+w, 3w=2y+z, hence x=9V/14, y=5V/14, z=4V/7, w=3V/7.

3. Execution & Resolution: I=[V+2(V−x)]/r=12V/(7r); R_AB=V/I=7r/12=7 Ω for r=12 Ω (option D). Current in AB is 7I/12, while each of the other two edges leaving A carries 5I/24. The earlier I/3 split was incorrect.
questions.check: Current conservation: 7I/12 + 2×(5I/24)=I.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q15 · SYNTHESIZE · D4 (Score 8)
questions.stem:
Twelve identical resistors, each of 8 Ω, form the edges of a cube. The equivalent resistance between the ends A and B of a face diagonal, as shown in Fig. 14, is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 14: 3D resistor cube of 12 edges (each 8 Ω) with terminals situated across face diagonal ends A and B.

hints.text: Terminals A and B are diagonally opposite corners on a single square face of the cube.
The plane passing through diagonal AB and perpendicular to that face is a mirror plane of symmetry. Nodes lying symmetrically across this plane share equal electric potentials.
The standard analytical result for the equivalent resistance across a face diagonal of a 12-edge cube of identical resistors r is R_face = (3/4) · r. Substitute r = 8 Ω.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Inject 1 A at A and withdraw it from B along a face diagonal of a 12-edge cube, with all edge resistances equal to r=8 Ω.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Solve the eight-node Kirchhoff equations. In units of r·I, the five distinct node potential levels are {0,1/4,3/8,1/2,3/4}: B=0, A=3/4, two opposite-face vertices at 1/4 and 1/2, and four remaining nodes at 3/8.
3. Execution & Resolution: Terminal drop is V_A−V_B=3rI/4, so R_AB=3r/4=6 Ω, option B. The previous claim that only four potential levels exist was incorrect.
questions.check: All eight Kirchhoff node equations hold for five potential levels and R_AB=6 Ω.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q16 · MODEL · D2 (Score 5)
questions.stem:
Six identical resistors, each of 10 Ω, form the edges of a tetrahedron ABCD, as shown in Fig. 15. The equivalent resistance between the corners A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 15: Regular tetrahedron ABCD with 6 identical 10 Ω edges across terminals A and B.

hints.text: A regular tetrahedron has 4 vertices (A, B, C, D) and 6 identical edges. Terminals are chosen at any two vertices, A and B.
Examine the symmetry of vertices C and D relative to the input and output terminals A and B. Vertices C and D are equidistant from A and equidistant from B.
By bilateral symmetry, V_C = V_D. Therefore, no current passes through the resistor along edge CD. Remove edge CD and calculate the remaining three parallel paths between A and B.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Six identical resistors of r = 10 Ω form the 6 edges of regular tetrahedron ABCD (AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD). External terminals are corners A and B.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Notice that vertices C and D are symmetrically situated with respect to both terminal A and terminal B (d(A,C) = d(A,D) = r, and d(B,C) = d(B,D) = r). By symmetry, V_C = V_D. Since the potential difference across edge CD is zero, resistor CD carries no current and can be removed.

3. Execution & Resolution: The remaining circuit between A and B consists of three parallel branches: Branch 1: direct edge AB with R_AB = r = 10 Ω. Branch 2: path ACB with R_ACB = r + r = 2r = 20 Ω. Branch 3: path ADB with R_ADB = r + r = 2r = 20 Ω. Combining in parallel: 1/R_eq = 1/r + 1/(2r) + 1/(2r) = 1/r + 1/r = 2/r. Hence, R_eq = r/2 = 10/2 = 5.0 Ω. Matches Option A.
questions.check: Tetrahedron topological invariance: Because all 4 vertices of a regular tetrahedron are mutually symmetric, the equivalent resistance between ANY pair of vertices is identically r/2 = 5 Ω.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q17 · APPLY · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem:
All the resistors in the ladder network of Fig. 16 are 8 Ω. The equivalent resistance between A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 16: Three-stage finite ladder network where all series and shunt resistors are 8 Ω.

hints.text: This is a finite ladder network with 3 sections. The most reliable method to solve finite ladders is to start from the far right end and collapse backward toward terminals A and B.
At the rightmost end, the series resistor and shunt resistor are in simple series. Combine them, then place that combination in parallel with the adjacent shunt resistor.
Step 1: (8 + 8) = 16 Ω. Step 2: 16||8 = 16/3 Ω. Step 3: Add middle series resistor: 16/3 + 8 = 40/3 Ω. Step 4: (40/3)||8 = 5 Ω. Step 5: Add input series resistor: 5 + 8 = 13 Ω.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The network is a 3-section finite ladder. Every resistor is R = 8 Ω. Terminals A and B are at the left input port.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Collapse the ladder sequentially from right to left: Section 3 (far right): The terminating 8 Ω series resistor and 8 Ω shunt resistor form a series branch: R_s3 = 8 + 8 = 16 Ω. This 16 Ω is in parallel with the second shunt resistor (8 Ω): R_p2 = (16 × 8)/(16 + 8) = 128/24 = 16/3 Ω.

3. Execution & Resolution: Add the middle 8 Ω series resistor: R_s2 = 8 + 16/3 = 40/3 Ω. This 40/3 Ω is in parallel with the first shunt resistor (8 Ω): R_p1 = ((40/3) × 8) / (40/3 + 8) = (320/3) / (64/3) = 320/64 = 5.0 Ω. Finally, add the first input series resistor (8 Ω): R_AB = 8 + R_p1 = 8 + 5 = 13.0 Ω. Matches Option A.
questions.check: Bounds check: Total resistance must be greater than the first series resistor (13 Ω > 8 Ω) and less than all series resistors combined (13 Ω < 24 Ω).

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q18 · MODEL · D3 (Score 6)
questions.stem:
The ladder network of Fig. 17 continues indefinitely, each section having a 4 Ω series resistor and a 3 Ω shunt resistor. The equivalent resistance between A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 17: Infinite ladder network with repeating sections of series 4 Ω and shunt 3 Ω extending indefinitely.

hints.text: The ladder is infinite, possessing self-similarity: removing or adding one repeating section (one 4 Ω series and one 3 Ω shunt) leaves the remainder identical to the original network.
Let the total equivalent resistance between A and B be R. The infinite tail after the first stage also has equivalent resistance R.
Write the self-consistent recursive equation: R = 4 + (3 × R)/(3 + R). Form the quadratic equation and solve for the physically positive root.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The ladder extends to infinity, with identical repeating unit cells having series resistance R_s = 4 Ω and shunt resistance R_p = 3 Ω. Let R_AB = R be the driving point resistance between input terminals A and B.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Due to infinite self-similarity, the entire sub-ladder to the right of the first shunt resistor has equivalent resistance equal to R. Thus, the circuit simplifies to a 4 Ω resistor in series with the parallel combination of a 3 Ω resistor and R: R = 4 + (3R)/(3 + R).

3. Execution & Resolution: Multiply through by (3 + R): R(3 + R) = 4(3 + R) + 3R => 3R + R² = 12 + 4R + 3R => R² - 4R - 12 = 0. Factor the quadratic: (R - 6)(R + 2) = 0. Since physical electrical resistance must be positive (R > 0), we reject R = -2 Ω and obtain R = 6.0 Ω. Matches Option D.
questions.check: Convergence check: Truncating after 1 stage: 4 + 3 = 7 Ω. After 2 stages: 4 + (3×7)/10 = 6.1 Ω. After 3 stages: 4 + (3×6.1)/9.1 = 6.01 Ω -> converges monotonically to 6.0 Ω.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q19 · JUSTIFY · D2 (Score 5)
questions.stem: Three resistors of 6 Ω each are used, all three in every arrangement, in any series and/or parallel combination. Which one of the following values of equivalent resistance CANNOT be obtained?
questions.figure_note: No diagram required; combinatorial topology proof.

hints.text: All three resistors of 6 Ω must be used simultaneously in each circuit configuration.
For 3 identical resistors of resistance R, there exist exactly 4 topologically distinct non-trivial two-terminal connection graphs.

Compute the equivalent resistance of all 4 topologies: (1) All series: 3R; (2) All parallel: R/3; (3) Two in parallel, in series with third: R/2 + R = 1.5R; (4) Two in series, in parallel with third: (2R || R) = 2R/3. Compare with the options.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Three identical resistors of R = 6 Ω are combined using all three elements in each arrangement. We seek the value that cannot be realized.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Enumerate all four possible topological combinations of 3 identical resistors: Case 1 (All three in series): R_eq = R + R + R = 3R = 3 × 6 = 18 Ω. Case 2 (All three in parallel): 1/R_eq = 1/R + 1/R + 1/R = 3/R => R_eq = R/3 = 6/3 = 2 Ω (Option B is obtainable). Case 3 (Two in parallel, in series with the third): R_eq = (R || R) + R = 3 + 6 = 9 Ω (Option D is obtainable). Case 4 (Two in series, in parallel with the third): R_eq = (R + R) || R = 12 || 6 = (12 × 6)/(12 + 6) = 72/18 = 4 Ω (Option C is obtainable).

3. Execution & Resolution: The complete set of achievable equivalent resistances is {2 Ω, 4 Ω, 9 Ω, 18 Ω}. The value 12 Ω is absent from this set (12 Ω would require only two 6 Ω resistors in series, but all three must be used). Therefore, 12 Ω CANNOT be obtained. Matches Option A.
questions.check: Combinatorial completeness check: Graph theory proves that there are exactly 4 series-parallel graphs on 3 labeled edges. No other topology exists.

questions.source_name: NSEJS Resistor Networks · L2-Q20 · JUSTIFY · D3 (Score 6)
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
options: A: Removing (open-circuiting) one resistor from a network can decrease the equivalent resistance between the terminals.
B: Two resistors connected in parallel can have an equivalent resistance greater than the larger of the two.
C: Connecting an extra resistor in parallel across any two points of a network cannot increase the equivalent resistance between the terminals of the network.
D: Replacing one resistor of a network by an ideal wire (short-circuiting it) cannot increase the equivalent resistance between the terminals of the network.
questions.answer: C, D: Connecting an extra resistor in parallel across any two points of a network cannot increase the equivalent resistance between the terminals of the network; Replacing one resistor of a network by an ideal wire (short-circuiting it) cannot increase the equivalent resistance between the terminals of the network
questions.figure_note: No diagram required; fundamental network monotonicity theorems.

hints.text: This question tests fundamental network theorems governing passive, linear, bilateral resistive networks (Rayleigh's Monotonicity Law).

Rayleigh's Monotonicity Law states that if the resistance of any element in a passive linear resistor network is decreased, the driving point equivalent resistance between any two external terminals cannot increase (it must either decrease or stay unchanged).

Evaluate each statement: Short-circuiting sets R_branch → 0 (a decrease), so R_eq cannot increase. Adding a parallel resistor decreases the effective resistance between those two nodes, so R_eq cannot increase.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Consider a general linear, passive, bilateral network of positive ohmic resistors. We assess the effect of network branch modifications on the driving point resistance R_eq between two external terminals.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: According to Rayleigh's Monotonicity Theorem (and Dirichlet's minimum dissipation principle), the driving point resistance R_eq of a passive resistive network is a monotonically increasing function of each individual branch resistance r_k: ∂R_eq/∂r_k ≥ 0 for all k.

3. Execution & Resolution: Statement A is FALSE: Removing a resistor corresponds to r_k → ∞ (increasing resistance). By monotonicity, R_eq can only increase or remain unchanged; it can NEVER decrease. Statement B is FALSE: In a parallel combination of two positive resistors R_1 and R_2, R_eq = (R_1 · R_2)/(R_1 + R_2) < min(R_1, R_2). It is strictly less than both resistors. Statement C is TRUE: Connecting a resistor in parallel across any two points reduces the impedance between those points (Δr ≤ 0). By monotonicity, the driving point resistance cannot increase (it must decrease or remain constant if those points were already equipotential). Statement D is TRUE: Short-circuiting a resistor replaces it with an ideal wire (r_k → 0). Since this is a reduction in resistance, the network equivalent resistance cannot increase. Thus, Statements C and D are correct.
questions.check: Energy dissipation check: Adding parallel paths or shorting resistors provides alternative current routes, which by Thomson's principle of minimum heat dissipation minimizes total network resistance.

questions.source_name: Grade9 authored Physics practice: Mechanics transfer
questions.stem: Two identical carts, each of mass m, are on a horizontal track. One cart moves at 8 m/s and collides head-on with the other cart initially at rest. They lock together. During the short collision, neglect the impulse of track friction. Afterwards, the joined carts slide on a rough horizontal section with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.25. Take g = 10 m/s². What distance do they travel after collision before stopping?
steps: 1. System and conservation choice: Over the short impact, horizontal external impulse is negligible. Horizontal momentum is conserved, but mechanical energy is not conserved because the carts stick.
2. Collision model: m(8) + m(0) = (2m)V gives V = 4 m/s immediately after impact.
3. After-collision braking: Kinetic-friction force is μ(2m)g, so deceleration a = μg = 2.5 m/s². Work–energy or v² = 2aL gives L = 4²/(2×2.5) = 3.2 m.
questions.check: Independent energy check: kinetic energy immediately after collision is (1/2)(2m)(4²) = 16m joules; friction does (0.25)(2m)(10)(3.2) = 16m joules of negative work. Initial kinetic energy was 32m joules; half was dissipated during sticking. Limits: as μ → 0⁺ the stopping distance diverges; doubling μ halves L. This is not an official examination question.

questions.source_name: Fluid Mechanics — Buoyancy in Accelerating Frames
questions.batch: Buoyant tension & relative acceleration in an elevator
questions.stem:
A solid block of density $\rho_s = 600\text{ kg/m}^3$ and mass $m = 3.0\text{ kg}$ is tied to the bottom of a container filled with water ($\rho_w = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3$) by a light inextensible cord. The entire container is placed inside an elevator accelerating vertically upwards with constant acceleration $a = 2.0\text{ m/s}^2$. Taking $g = 10.0\text{ m/s}^2$:

Determine the tension $T$ in the cord during upward acceleration, and the initial upward acceleration $a_{\text{rel}}$ of the block relative to the container immediately after the cord is severed.
steps: 1. In the upward accelerating elevator frame, effective gravity is g_eff = g + a = 10.0 + 2.0 = 12.0 m/s².
2. Block volume V = m / ρ_s = 3.0 / 600 = 0.0050 m³. Buoyant force F_B = ρ_w * V * g_eff = 1000 * 0.0050 * 12.0 = 60.0 N.
3. Effective weight W_eff = m * g_eff = 3.0 * 12.0 = 36.0 N.
4. Equilibrium gives tension T = F_B - W_eff = 60.0 - 36.0 = 24.0 N.
5. Immediately after cord is cut, net upward force F_net = 24.0 N; relative acceleration a_rel = F_net / m = 24.0 / 3.0 = 8.0 m/s².
questions.check: Limiting check: as elevator acceleration a -> -g (free fall), g_eff -> 0, giving T = 0 N and a_rel = 0 m/s².

questions.source_name: Fluid Mechanics — Droplet Coalescence & Surface Energy Release
questions.batch: Non-linear geometric scaling & surface energy release
questions.stem:
1000 identical spherical water droplets, each of radius $r = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}$, coalesce into a single spherical drop. The surface tension of water is $T = 0.075\text{ N/m}$.

Calculate the net decrease in total surface area and the surface energy released during coalescence.
steps: 1. Volume conservation: (4/3)πR³ = 1000 * (4/3)πr³ => R = 10r = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m.
2. Initial surface area A_i = 1000 * 4πr² = 4000πr².
3. Final surface area A_f = 4πR² = 4π(10r)² = 400πr².
4. Area reduction ΔA = A_i - A_f = 3600πr² = 3.6π × 10⁻⁵ m² ≈ 1.131 × 10⁻⁴ m².
5. Released surface energy ΔU = T * ΔA = 0.075 * 1.131 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 8.48 × 10⁻⁶ J.
questions.check: Limiting fraction: ΔU / U_i = 1 - N^(-1/3) = 1 - 0.1 = 90% of surface energy released.
